modules.title: Rights, restrictions and remedies
modules.description: Identify the right-holder, the restriction and the constitutional remedy before choosing an option.
modules.prerequisite: No prerequisite; read the core rule before attempting the application.

sections.heading: Start with the right-holder
sections.body: Read a rights question in three passes: who claims protection, what the State has done, and which provision governs it. Article 14 protects persons, whereas the freedoms in Article 19 are framed for citizens. Article 21 protects life and personal liberty of persons. These differences matter even when every option mentions a familiar right. Article 20 separately addresses retrospective criminal punishment, repeated prosecution and punishment for the same offence, and compelled self-incrimination. Article 22 supplies arrest and detention safeguards with specified exceptions. Build a small article map, but do not turn the map into an automatic answer key: the precise facts and the provision's qualifications still control the result.

sections.heading: A right and its limits travel together
sections.body: A statement that freedom exists is incomplete without asking what restrictions the Constitution permits. For expression, examine Article 19(1)(a) together with Article 19(2); the grounds in the latter are not interchangeable with the restriction clauses for other freedoms. A plausible public-interest label is not enough by itself to establish a permitted restriction. Likewise, Article 21 speaks to deprivation under legally established procedure, while particular judicial standards require their own checked authorities. In a passage question, separate the passage's account of a right from a wider constitutional proposition. During revision, write a right in one column, its holder in another, and the linked restriction clause in a third. Then test one altered factual situation.

sections.heading: Choose the remedy by its jurisdiction
sections.body: Article 32 gives access to the Supreme Court for enforcement of Part III rights. Article 226 gives High Courts power to issue directions, orders or writs for Part III enforcement and for other purposes, subject to its territorial and jurisdictional requirements. Therefore, a claim about an ordinary legal right is not automatically an Article 32 claim merely because the requested remedy is called a writ. Article 37 states that Directive Principles are not enforceable by any court, while also describing their importance in governance. Article 300A protects property through a constitutional provision outside Part III. Practise classifying the right first, then the appropriate jurisdiction; avoid treating all constitutional provisions as fundamental rights.

distinctions.contrast: The former concerns Part III enforcement in the Supreme Court; the latter gives High Courts wider subject scope, with its own jurisdictional requirements.
Article 14 protects persons; Article 19 freedoms are framed for citizens.

pitfalls: Do not transfer Article 19(2) grounds to every other Article 19 freedom.
Do not call every constitutional right a Part III fundamental right.
A passage link does not prove that all required legal knowledge appears inside the passage.

modules.title: Institutions, ordinances and legislative power
modules.description: Separate the actor, source of power, procedural condition and limit.
modules.prerequisite: No prerequisite; read the core rule before attempting the application.

sections.heading: Map the constitutional actor
sections.body: Institution questions often become manageable when the actor is identified before the action. Article 79 describes Parliament as consisting of the President and the two Houses. Article 74 addresses the Council of Ministers' aid and advice to the President, including the reconsideration proviso. Do not substitute the everyday description of an institution for its constitutional composition. Similarly, distinguish a constitutional office from the person temporarily holding it, and executive functions from legislative functions. Create a four-column map: actor, article, power and condition. Retrieve the map from memory, then check it. The goal is not to memorise isolated numbers but to recognise when a question gives the correct power to the wrong office.

sections.heading: Ordinances have conditions and an expiry structure
sections.body: Under Article 123, the President's ordinance power depends on the specified parliamentary recess condition and satisfaction that circumstances require immediate action. An ordinance has the force and effect of an Act of Parliament, but is subject to constitutional limits and must be laid before both Houses. It ceases to operate after the constitutional period following reassembly unless it ends earlier by the specified events. Article 213 concerns the Governor's ordinance power and has additional conditions that must be read in its own text. Do not assume an ordinance is a permanent replacement for legislation or is unlimited because it is executive-issued. In a hypothetical, check the sitting condition before moving to duration or legislative competence.

sections.heading: Competence is different from inconsistency
sections.body: Article 246 distributes legislative subject-matter power through the Union, State and Concurrent Lists, with its stated priority rules. Article 254 addresses inconsistency between parliamentary and State laws in its specified field, including the presidential-assent arrangement and Parliament's later overriding power. These are related but different questions: first ask whether the legislature had competence; then ask whether the particular inconsistency rule applies. Article 141 separately states the binding force of law declared by the Supreme Court for courts within India. It does not say that every factual sentence or passing observation is a statutory rule. Practise distinguishing actor, field and legal effect rather than choosing a familiar article simply because it appears in the options.

distinctions.contrast: Competence asks who can legislate on the field; Article 254 asks about the specified inconsistency between laws.
Both can have legislative force, but an ordinance has special promulgation and continuation conditions.

pitfalls: A recess condition is not the same as a general emergency proclamation.
Do not equate Article 254 presidential assent with permanent immunity from Parliament.
Read Governor and President ordinance powers separately.

modules.title: Utility, legal validity and legal reasoning
modules.description: Recognise the claim a theorist makes rather than matching names mechanically.
modules.prerequisite: No prerequisite; read the core rule before attempting the application.

sections.heading: Bentham asks about consequences
sections.body: Bentham's principle of utility evaluates actions and government measures by their tendency to increase or diminish happiness for those affected. Community welfare is understood through the interests of its members rather than as an unexplained independent entity. His account therefore asks about consequences, including benefits and harms, rather than treating the decision-maker's approval as its own justification. In the felicific-calculus discussion, intensity, duration, certainty and nearness concern a pleasure or pain; fecundity, purity and extent widen the assessment. For revision, connect each term to a small policy example. Do not assume that naming utility settles the best policy: comparing real consequences still requires facts, uncertainty and attention to all affected people.

sections.heading: Separate existence from evaluation
sections.body: Hart's 1958 discussion defends distinguishing what law is from what law ought to be. That distinction permits an identified law to be morally criticised; it does not establish that every enacted command deserves moral approval. Nor does it mean legal systems never contain moral standards. In a passage, identify whether the writer is describing a test of legal validity, defending a moral standard, or advocating reform. The rest is a reading exercise: underline the proposition actually asserted, rewrite it without the author's name, and compare it with each option. Avoid adding a stronger claim such as automatic obedience or complete separation of every legal and moral issue.

sections.heading: Turn a theory into a comparison task
sections.body: A useful comparison matrix records the question a theory is answering, the criterion it offers, and what it leaves open. Bentham's welfare evaluation and a positivist inquiry into legal existence need not answer the same question. A policy can be legally valid yet criticised for its effects; a proposal can promote welfare yet still require enactment before becoming a legal rule. These examples are reasoning exercises, not a complete account of every school's views. When reading an unfamiliar extract, mark its conclusion, supporting reasons, assumptions and limiting words. Then test an option by asking whether it restates the author's claim, contradicts it, or goes beyond the passage. This is more robust than learning a name-to-slogan list alone.

distinctions.contrast: Identifying a rule as law is conceptually distinguishable from judging whether it is just or desirable.
A utilitarian assessment asks about effects on welfare rather than treating the evaluator's dislike as decisive.

pitfalls: Do not infer that positivism requires approval of every existing law.
A thinker's name is context, not a substitute for reading the precise claim.
Do not turn Bentham's calculus into an asserted scientifically certain forecast.

modules.title: Natural justice and fair procedure
modules.description: Distinguish the right to be heard from the requirement of an impartial decision-maker.
modules.prerequisite: No prerequisite; read the core rule before attempting the application.

sections.heading: Two questions about the decision-maker
sections.body: Natural-justice problems commonly ask whether the decision-maker is impartial and whether the affected person received a fair opportunity to respond. The traditional labels are nemo judex in causa sua and audi alteram partem. They identify different defects: a complete hearing does not necessarily cure disqualifying bias, and an unbiased official can still deny a fair hearing. The Supreme Court's discussion in the 12 May 2023 judgment explains these anchors and links procedural fairness to constitutional guarantees. For an exam scenario, write down who decided, what interest or role that person had, what material mattered and what opportunity was given. Diagnose the defect before choosing a Latin expression or a remedy.

sections.heading: An opportunity must address the case to be met
sections.body: Hearing is not a decorative invitation. Notice of the material case, relevant adverse material and a meaningful opportunity to answer help make it effective. At the same time, natural justice is contextual: its application is not an identical checklist for every kind of administrative action. The January 2025 Supreme Court discussion emphasises the core of reasonable procedure and the circumstances in which fairness is assessed. Do not invent an unconditional rule that every action requires a full oral trial, cross-examination or identical time limits. In a passage problem, use the procedural standard expressly stated there, then identify exactly which fact satisfies or defeats it. Distinguish a denied opportunity from an opportunity that was available but not used.

sections.heading: Review process and legal limits, not personal preference
sections.body: Administrative-law revision should distinguish the fairness of the procedure from whether the final outcome seems attractive. A successful result for one person does not prove that the process was fair, and disagreement with the result does not itself identify a legal defect. In a fictional licensing problem, ask separately about the statutory power, notice, adverse material, impartiality and reasons supplied by the problem. Do not assume a court may replace the authority's view merely because another view seems better. For a recall drill, explain the defect in one sentence, then change one fact: provide adequate notice, remove the interested decision-maker, or disclose the adverse report. Describe which concern changes and which concern remains.

distinctions.contrast: Audi alteram partem addresses a fair opportunity to answer; nemo judex addresses the decision-maker's conflicting role or interest.
Losing on the merits is not itself proof of a procedural violation.

pitfalls: Do not assume every hearing must be oral or resemble a criminal trial.
A hearing does not automatically remove a separate bias concern.
Treat exceptions and urgency as context-sensitive legal questions, not universal shortcuts.

modules.title: Criminal liability and the statute-version trap
modules.description: Identify the governing enactment, offence ingredients and possible exception separately.
modules.prerequisite: No prerequisite; read the core rule before attempting the application.

sections.heading: Attach every section number to its enactment
sections.body: The BNS, BNSS and BSA address substantive criminal law, criminal procedure and evidence respectively. Historical questions may instead name the IPC, CrPC or Indian Evidence Act. A familiar section number without the statute name can therefore mislead. Use the official correspondence tables as navigation aids, not as proof that every old provision was copied unchanged. For an older factual problem, examine the law specified by the question and any relevant commencement or savings provision; do not silently substitute a newer section. Keep a version label on every revision card. The present module teaches selected BNS basics and does not claim that all criminal proceedings or all earlier facts are governed by a single new enactment.

sections.heading: Ingredients first, exceptions second
sections.body: For any offence, separate the prohibited conduct, relevant mental element, required consequence and any accompanying conditions. Then check possible general or special exceptions. BNS section 3(1) makes the general-exceptions chapter relevant to offence definitions even where an exception is not repeated each time. Section 2(11) connects good faith to due care and attention, so a bare claim of honesty is not the whole statutory inquiry. Sections 14 and 17 distinguish certain good-faith mistakes of fact relating to legal duty or justification from mistakes of law. In a problem, identify the mistaken fact precisely. A mistaken opinion that a known act is lawful is not automatically the same kind of mistake.

sections.heading: Avoid category collapse
sections.body: BNS section 100 defines culpable homicide and section 101 defines when culpable homicide is murder, subject to the latter's exceptions. Read the statutory conditions before choosing between these categories; the bare fact that a death occurred does not answer the classification. Similarly, section 3(5) addresses a criminal act done by several persons in furtherance of their common intention, not automatic guilt merely from proximity. Section 4 includes community service among the listed punishments, but that does not make it available for every offence. Build contrast cards that state both the rule and its limit. Do not confuse an available punishment, an offence definition and a rule attributing responsibility: they perform different jobs in the analysis.

distinctions.contrast: BNS supplies substantive offences and punishments; BNSS supplies criminal procedure.
The specified BNS good-faith exceptions recognise particular mistakes of fact, not a general excuse for misunderstanding law.

pitfalls: Never memorise a section number without its enactment and version.
Honest belief alone is not BNS good faith without due care and attention.
Neither death nor presence at a scene by itself establishes every ingredient of the alleged offence.

modules.title: Relevance, proof and confessions
modules.description: Separate whether a fact matters from whether a particular form of proof may be used.
modules.prerequisite: No prerequisite; read the core rule before attempting the application.

sections.heading: Relevance is not the whole proof question
sections.body: Evidence questions often contain two layers: whether a fact is relevant and whether the proposed method of proving it is legally permitted. BSA section 3 concerns evidence of facts in issue and relevant facts. Sections 54 and 55 address oral evidence and its directness; the document provisions distinguish primary and secondary evidence and specify their treatment. Do not infer that every relevant statement is admissible regardless of the rule governing it. Electronic or digital records require attention to the applicable provisions, including sections 61 to 63, rather than a slogan that all screenshots are automatically sufficient. Start by naming the fact to be established, then the evidence offered, then the rule controlling that form of proof.

sections.heading: Confessions have separate exclusion rules
sections.body: BSA section 22 concerns confessions affected by the specified inducement, threat, coercion or promise and contains provisos. Section 23 separately deals with confessions to police officers and confessions while in police custody, including the Magistrate condition and the limited discovery proviso. These rules should not be merged into an assumption that a confession becomes admissible merely because somebody calls it voluntary. The discovery proviso is limited to the part of information distinctly related to the discovered fact; it is not permission to prove an entire narrative automatically. In revision, separate the recipient, custody status, circumstances of making the statement and the precise portion sought to be proved. Each may trigger a different question.

sections.heading: Burden and version belong in the answer
sections.body: BSA section 104 places the burden of proving asserted facts on the person seeking judgment dependent on them; section 105 offers the practical test of who would fail if no evidence were given on either side. Specific statutory presumptions or exceptions may require further analysis, so this starting rule is not a complete answer to every burden question. Section 170 contains repeal and savings provisions, including a rule concerning matters pending immediately before commencement. That makes the date and procedural context important when moving from an Indian Evidence Act question to BSA revision. Keep old and new section labels side by side, but do not claim that a correspondence table determines the applicable law for every proceeding.

distinctions.contrast: A fact may matter logically while a legal rule restricts how it can be proved.
The discovery proviso does not automatically admit the whole accompanying narrative.

pitfalls: A voluntary confession to a police officer is not automatically provable.
Do not assume every digital copy bypasses the applicable proof requirements.
Read savings before applying BSA to a proceeding already pending at commencement.

modules.title: Formation, consent and remedies
modules.description: Move from agreement to enforceability, then select the legally appropriate remedy.
modules.prerequisite: No prerequisite; read the core rule before attempting the application.

sections.heading: Agreement is the start, not the conclusion
sections.body: The Contract Act distinguishes a proposal, acceptance, promise, consideration, agreement and contract. Section 10 makes enforceability depend on factors including competent parties, free consent, lawful consideration and object, and absence of an express rule making the agreement void. Sections 7 and 8 address acceptance, including an unqualified acceptance and acceptance through performance in the stated circumstances. Avoid the shortcut that any discussion of price or any document headed agreement must be an enforceable contract. Ask what was proposed, how assent occurred, whether the parties had capacity and whether the law permits enforcement. The facts may establish only some of these elements. An exam option that supplies a missing element without factual support should be treated cautiously.

sections.heading: Consent, consideration and legality are distinct
sections.body: Section 13 addresses agreement on the same thing in the same sense, while section 14 identifies conditions for free consent. A problem can therefore involve consent but still require analysis of coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation or mistake. Section 2(d) allows consideration to move from the promisee or another person at the promisor's desire; do not import the different English-law formula. Section 23 concerns unlawful consideration and objects. Section 25 provides the general rule about agreements without consideration with stated exceptions. Keep these inquiries separate: payment does not cure an unlawful object, and an absence of cash does not prove an absence of legally recognised consideration. Read the exact exception rather than inventing a general fairness exception.

sections.heading: A remedy is not an automatic windfall
sections.body: Section 73 addresses compensation for losses naturally arising from breach or within the parties' contemplation at formation and excludes remote and indirect losses in its stated terms. Section 74 concerns reasonable compensation where a sum or penalty is stipulated, with the named amount acting as a ceiling rather than an automatic entitlement to the maximum. Specific Relief Act section 10 addresses enforcement of specific performance subject to the provisions it identifies. An order to perform and an award of money are different forms of relief; the governing conditions matter. In a problem, identify breach, the causal loss, the applicable limitation and the requested remedy. For historical questions, check the relevant version instead of importing a later statutory formulation without explanation.

distinctions.contrast: A contract is an agreement enforceable by law; an agreement may fail an enforceability condition.
Section 74 concerns reasonable compensation within the statutory ceiling, not an automatic maximum.

pitfalls: Do not treat consideration as necessarily cash or necessarily supplied only by the promisee.
A serious breach does not make every remote consequence recoverable.
Do not reuse an old specific-performance formula without checking the applicable version.

modules.title: Negligence and consumer protection
modules.description: Separate liability elements, consumer status and the requested relief.
modules.prerequisite: No prerequisite; read the core rule before attempting the application.

sections.heading: Build the negligence chain
sections.body: A basic negligence inquiry asks about a duty of care, breach and resulting legally recognised damage causally connected with that breach. The Supreme Court's reproduction of the negligence principles in the 3 June 2021 judgment supplies this structure and also warns that professional-negligence questions have additional considerations. Do not infer liability simply because an unfortunate result occurred. In an ordinary fictional scenario, identify the relationship creating the duty, the conduct alleged to fall below the required standard and the link to the injury. Then ask what defence or special rule the question provides. This module does not equate every error of judgment with professional negligence or turn civil standards into criminal standards automatically.

sections.heading: Consumer status depends on statutory definitions
sections.body: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 defines consumer through acquisition of goods or hiring or availing services for consideration, including specified approved users or beneficiaries. Its commercial-purpose exclusion and the explanation for goods used exclusively for livelihood through self-employment must be read carefully. The statutory service definition excludes service free of charge and under a contract of personal service. Do not decide consumer status merely by whether an institution is public or private, or whether the claimant likes the service. Identify the transaction, consideration, purpose and relevant definition. Complex mixed-service or medical-service issues may require checked case law; these are not settled by an oversimplified card claiming that every service of a particular label is covered.

sections.heading: Defect, deficiency and relief are separate
sections.body: The Act distinguishes a defect in goods from a deficiency in services, and its relief provisions identify remedies that consumer commissions may grant within the statutory framework. The Central Consumer Protection Authority and the dispute-redressal commissions are not interchangeable labels for the same body. A strong answer identifies the complained-of goods or service, the alleged shortcoming and the requested remedy before selecting the institution or statutory term. Monetary jurisdiction rules can change, so this sprint deliberately avoids teaching unverified thresholds. In practice, compare replacing a faulty product, correcting a service deficiency and awarding compensation: the objective and legal basis differ. Do not assume every breach creates the same remedy or that consumer remedies eliminate every other legal route.

distinctions.contrast: The statutory vocabulary generally distinguishes shortcomings in goods from shortcomings in services.
The CCPA has consumer-protection regulatory functions; commissions adjudicate consumer disputes within their statutory jurisdiction.

pitfalls: An accident alone does not prove all negligence elements.
The livelihood/self-employment explanation is not an unlimited exemption for every business purchase.
Do not learn outdated monetary jurisdiction thresholds from an unchecked summary.

flashcards.prompt: Does Article 14 protect only citizens?
flashcards.answer: No. Its text protects any person against the specified State denial of equality and equal protection.
flashcards.why: Check the right-holder before assessing a restriction.

flashcards.prompt: Who holds the Article 19 freedoms?
flashcards.answer: Article 19 frames its listed freedoms for citizens. Do not assume every Part III provision uses the same holder.
flashcards.why: Person and citizen are not interchangeable.

flashcards.prompt: Which restriction clause goes with freedom of expression?
flashcards.answer: Read Article 19(1)(a) with Article 19(2). The restriction clauses for other freedoms are not automatically identical.
flashcards.why: A correct freedom paired with the wrong limitation is a common distractor.

flashcards.prompt: What does Article 20 protect against?
flashcards.answer: It separately addresses retrospective criminal punishment, repeated prosecution and punishment for the same offence, and compelled self-incrimination. Each clause has its own requirements.
flashcards.why: Recognise the particular clause instead of choosing a broad slogan.

flashcards.prompt: What is the subject scope of Article 32?
flashcards.answer: Article 32 concerns enforcement of Part III rights through the Supreme Court. It is not a general original remedy for every ordinary legal claim.
flashcards.why: First classify the right, then the jurisdiction.

flashcards.prompt: How is Article 226 broader in subject scope?
flashcards.answer: High Courts can issue the specified directions, orders and writs for Part III enforcement and other purposes. Territorial and other jurisdictional conditions still matter.
flashcards.why: Broader scope does not mean unlimited jurisdiction.

flashcards.prompt: Are Directive Principles directly court-enforceable under Article 37?
flashcards.answer: Article 37 says they are not enforceable by any court. It also identifies their fundamental role in governance and legislative application.
flashcards.why: Non-enforceability is not a statement of irrelevance.

flashcards.prompt: Is Article 300A within Part III?
flashcards.answer: No. Its property protection is a constitutional provision outside Part III, so do not label it a fundamental right merely because it appears in the Constitution.
flashcards.why: Constitutional right and Part III right are different categories.

flashcards.prompt: What comprises Parliament under Article 79?
flashcards.answer: The President and the two Houses comprise Parliament. Do not omit the President when answering a question about constitutional composition.
flashcards.why: Composition differs from who debates or votes in a House.

flashcards.prompt: What does Article 74 concern?
flashcards.answer: It concerns the Council of Ministers aiding and advising the President. Read its reconsideration proviso rather than assuming the text contains no qualification.
flashcards.why: The provision and its proviso should be recalled together.

flashcards.prompt: When is the Article 123 sitting-condition barrier engaged?
flashcards.answer: The power cannot be exercised when both Houses of Parliament are in session. The immediate-action satisfaction requirement must also be met.
flashcards.why: Both is not equivalent to either.

flashcards.prompt: Does an ordinance have the force of an Act?
flashcards.answer: Article 123 gives it the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament subject to constitutional conditions. That does not make its continuation indefinite.
flashcards.why: Legal effect and duration are separate inquiries.

flashcards.prompt: What is the normal Article 123 post-reassembly time limit?
flashcards.answer: The ordinance ceases to operate six weeks after reassembly, unless it ends earlier under the provision. Where the Houses reassemble on different dates, the later date is used for that period.
flashcards.why: The trigger is reassembly, not simply the original promulgation date.

flashcards.prompt: What is the core job of Article 246?
flashcards.answer: It distributes legislative subject-matter competence through the Lists with stated priority rules. Start with the field of legislation before applying an inconsistency rule.
flashcards.why: Who may legislate and which law prevails are not the same question.

flashcards.prompt: Does Article 254(2) assent permanently prevent Parliament from legislating?
flashcards.answer: No. The proviso preserves Parliament's power to make a law on the matter, including adding to, amending, varying or repealing the State law.
flashcards.why: A qualified exception is not permanent immunity.

flashcards.prompt: What does Article 141 make binding on courts within India?
flashcards.answer: It makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding. Do not read it as turning every factual remark into legislation.
flashcards.why: Find the legal proposition, not merely a sentence containing a case name.

flashcards.prompt: What is Bentham's principle of utility testing?
flashcards.answer: It evaluates an action or government measure by its tendency to increase or diminish happiness for those affected. Personal approval alone is not the criterion.
flashcards.why: Identify the evaluative standard in the passage.

flashcards.prompt: How does Bentham connect community interest with individual interests?
flashcards.answer: He explains community interest through the interests of its members. The community is not an unexplained independent source of pleasure or pain.
flashcards.why: Avoid replacing individual effects with an empty collective label.

flashcards.prompt: Which four calculus factors first concern a pleasure or pain considered by itself?
flashcards.answer: Intensity, duration, certainty and nearness are the initial factors. The wider assessment also considers further consequences and affected persons.
flashcards.why: Separate the initial factors from later dimensions.

flashcards.prompt: What do fecundity and purity ask about in Bentham's account?
flashcards.answer: Fecundity concerns the chance of consequences of the same kind, while purity concerns not being followed by the opposite kind. They concern the tendency of the producing act or event in his explanation.
flashcards.why: Similar-looking technical terms express different questions.

flashcards.prompt: What does extent add to Bentham's calculation?
flashcards.answer: It brings in the number of people affected. An assessment of a public measure therefore cannot simply stop with one person's benefit.
flashcards.why: A community question requires attention to affected persons.

flashcards.prompt: Does identifying a rule as legally valid show that it is morally good?
flashcards.answer: No. The distinction defended in Hart's 1958 discussion permits law to be identified and still morally criticised.
flashcards.why: Do not confuse a validity inquiry with approval.

flashcards.prompt: How should you test an inference option in a theory passage?
flashcards.answer: Ask whether it follows from the stated premises without adding a new assumption. A plausible policy preference may still go beyond the author's argument.
flashcards.why: This is an original reading method, not a quotation or a legal rule.

flashcards.prompt: What should a theory comparison sheet record?
flashcards.answer: Record the question asked, the criterion supplied and the conclusion actually defended. Two theories may address different questions rather than contradicting each other on every point.
flashcards.why: Compare propositions before comparing labels.

flashcards.prompt: What does audi alteram partem address?
flashcards.answer: It addresses a fair opportunity for the affected person to answer the case. The suitable form of that opportunity depends on context.
flashcards.why: Do not assume every hearing must have one identical format.

flashcards.prompt: What does nemo judex in causa sua address?
flashcards.answer: It addresses the requirement of an impartial decision-maker. Giving a hearing does not itself remove a separate disqualifying-interest concern.
flashcards.why: Hearing and impartiality are distinct anchors.

flashcards.prompt: Can an unbiased authority still deny natural justice?
flashcards.answer: Yes. It can fail to provide a fair opportunity to address the material case even if no bias is alleged.
flashcards.why: One satisfied requirement does not prove the other.

flashcards.prompt: Is a fair hearing always an oral trial?
flashcards.answer: No. The required procedure is context-sensitive rather than a universal requirement of a full trial.
flashcards.why: Avoid treating one procedural form as compulsory in all settings.

flashcards.prompt: Why does notice matter?
flashcards.answer: A person needs to know the material case that calls for an answer. An invitation that conceals the decisive adverse case may not provide a meaningful opportunity.
flashcards.why: Examine the content of the opportunity, not its label.

flashcards.prompt: Does losing prove unfair procedure?
flashcards.answer: No. A lawful adverse result and a procedural defect are separate matters.
flashcards.why: Identify the actual unfairness alleged.

flashcards.prompt: Does a favourable outcome establish that the process was fair?
flashcards.answer: Not necessarily. Procedural fairness is not reduced to whether one party liked the result.
flashcards.why: Outcome and process must be analysed independently.

flashcards.prompt: What is a useful one-sentence diagnosis for a hearing problem?
flashcards.answer: Identify the adverse material and the missing opportunity to answer it. Then test whether a changed procedural fact addresses that specific concern.
flashcards.why: This is a study method grounded in the fairness issues, not a universal remedy rule.

flashcards.prompt: What are the different jobs of BNS, BNSS and BSA?
flashcards.answer: BNS concerns substantive criminal law, BNSS criminal procedure and BSA evidence. A section number must be attached to the enactment.
flashcards.why: Do not answer a procedural question from an offence-definition card.

flashcards.prompt: Do correspondence tables prove that old and new provisions are identical?
flashcards.answer: No. They are navigation aids; compare the actual wording and applicable commencement or savings provisions.
flashcards.why: A mapped section may still have changes or a different temporal application.

flashcards.prompt: Must BNS general exceptions be repeated in every offence definition to matter?
flashcards.answer: No. Section 3(1) makes offence definitions and penal provisions subject to the general-exceptions chapter.
flashcards.why: Read the offence together with the applicable exception.

flashcards.prompt: Is sincere belief alone sufficient for BNS good faith?
flashcards.answer: No. Section 2(11) makes due care and attention part of the inquiry.
flashcards.why: Honesty and statutory good faith are not automatically identical.

flashcards.prompt: What is the key fact/law distinction in BNS sections 14 and 17?
flashcards.answer: The specified good-faith exceptions address mistakes of fact connected with duty or justification. They do not create a general defence of misunderstanding the law.
flashcards.why: Name the fact believed, rather than merely asserting ignorance.

flashcards.prompt: Does a death automatically establish murder under BNS?
flashcards.answer: No. Apply the ingredients of culpable homicide in section 100 and the murder conditions and exceptions in section 101.
flashcards.why: A result does not supply every legal condition.

flashcards.prompt: What is required by BNS section 3(5), beyond several persons being present?
flashcards.answer: The criminal act must be done in furtherance of their common intention as specified by the section. Mere presence is not the complete statutory test.
flashcards.why: Do not replace the stated responsibility rule with association alone.

flashcards.prompt: Is community service listed among BNS punishments?
flashcards.answer: Yes, section 4 lists it. Availability for a particular offence still requires the applicable provision.
flashcards.why: A listed punishment is not an automatic option in every case.

flashcards.prompt: Does logical relevance automatically settle admissibility?
flashcards.answer: No. Identify the relevant fact and then the rule controlling the proposed form of proof.
flashcards.why: A relevant proposition can face a separate proof restriction.

flashcards.prompt: What is the starting point for BSA oral evidence?
flashcards.answer: Sections 54 and 55 address proof through oral evidence and its directness. Read them with any applicable special rule rather than assuming every reported statement qualifies.
flashcards.why: Source and form of testimony matter.

flashcards.prompt: Does voluntariness alone permit proof of a confession to a police officer?
flashcards.answer: No. BSA section 23(1) separately restricts proof of a confession made to a police officer against the accused.
flashcards.why: Do not merge sections 22 and 23 into one voluntariness test.

flashcards.prompt: What does BSA section 22 address?
flashcards.answer: It addresses confessions affected by the specified inducement, threat, coercion or promise. Its stated conditions and provisos must also be read.
flashcards.why: The source and effect of the pressure matter.

flashcards.prompt: Does the discovery proviso admit the entire accompanying narrative?
flashcards.answer: No. Section 23 limits proof to the information distinctly related to the discovered fact in the specified custody circumstances.
flashcards.why: Partial admissibility does not become wholesale admissibility.

flashcards.prompt: Where does the general burden of proving asserted facts begin?
flashcards.answer: BSA section 104 places it on the person seeking a judgment dependent on those facts. Particular statutory rules may require further analysis.
flashcards.why: State the starting rule without denying possible exceptions.

flashcards.prompt: What practical test does BSA section 105 use?
flashcards.answer: Ask which party would fail if no evidence were given on either side. This helps locate the burden at the relevant stage.
flashcards.why: Use the legal issue, not which side speaks first.

flashcards.prompt: Why must a pending older proceeding be checked before using BSA?
flashcards.answer: Section 170 contains a savings rule for specified pending matters. A newer statute name does not by itself settle the law governing every proceeding.
flashcards.why: Do not erase temporal context from an old paper.

flashcards.prompt: When does an agreement become a contract?
flashcards.answer: When it is enforceable by law. Section 10 supplies key enforceability conditions rather than making every agreement a contract.
flashcards.why: An agreement is not the end of the analysis.

flashcards.prompt: What does section 7 require of acceptance?
flashcards.answer: Acceptance must be absolute and unqualified, with the provision's rules about manner. A counter-proposal does not simply repeat the original acceptance.
flashcards.why: Check whether the purported assent changes the terms.

flashcards.prompt: Must consideration move only from the promisee?
flashcards.answer: No. Under section 2(d), it may move from the promisee or another person at the promisor's desire.
flashcards.why: Do not import a different jurisdiction's formula.

flashcards.prompt: Does section 25 say that lack of consideration always ends the case?
flashcards.answer: No. It contains stated exceptions to its general rule. The facts must satisfy an actual exception, not a general feeling of fairness.
flashcards.why: Learn the exception with the rule.

flashcards.prompt: How do consent and free consent differ?
flashcards.answer: Section 13 concerns agreement on the same thing in the same sense. Section 14 separately identifies conditions for free consent.
flashcards.why: Agreement and freedom from vitiating factors are distinct.

flashcards.prompt: Can payment cure an unlawful object?
flashcards.answer: Not merely by existing. Section 23 separately tests lawfulness of the consideration and object.
flashcards.why: One formation element cannot replace another.

flashcards.prompt: Are all consequences of breach recoverable under section 73?
flashcards.answer: No. The provision addresses its specified natural or contemplated losses and excludes remote and indirect loss in its stated terms.
flashcards.why: Loss, causation and remoteness all matter.

flashcards.prompt: Does a section 74 named amount automatically become the award?
flashcards.answer: No. The provision concerns reasonable compensation not exceeding the specified sum or penalty.
flashcards.why: A ceiling is not a guaranteed maximum award.

flashcards.prompt: What is the basic negligence chain?
flashcards.answer: Duty of care, breach and resulting legally recognised damage causally connected with the breach. An adverse outcome alone does not establish the chain.
flashcards.why: Name the missing link in a factual question.

flashcards.prompt: Does an accident necessarily prove professional negligence?
flashcards.answer: No. Professional-negligence questions require their appropriate standards and circumstances.
flashcards.why: Do not equate every error or bad result with legal fault.

flashcards.prompt: Does consumer status require checking consideration?
flashcards.answer: Yes. The statutory definition connects acquisition of goods or services with consideration and specified approved users or beneficiaries.
flashcards.why: An everyday customer label is not the whole legal test.

flashcards.prompt: What is the livelihood/self-employment explanation about?
flashcards.answer: It qualifies the commercial-purpose exclusion for the specified goods bought and used exclusively to earn livelihood through self-employment. It is not a blanket business exemption.
flashcards.why: Keep the statutory limits attached to the exception.

flashcards.prompt: What does the Act call a shortcoming in goods?
flashcards.answer: The statutory term is defect within its definition. Do not automatically use the service-specific vocabulary for every goods complaint.
flashcards.why: Terminology can identify the object of the complaint.

flashcards.prompt: What does deficiency generally concern?
flashcards.answer: It concerns the statutory shortcoming in the quality, nature or manner of performance of a service. Establish the relevant obligation and alleged shortcoming.
flashcards.why: Mere dissatisfaction is not the full definition.

flashcards.prompt: Are free services and a contract of personal service included without qualification?
flashcards.answer: No. The service definition contains exclusions for service free of charge and under a contract of personal service.
flashcards.why: Read the definition before deciding coverage.

flashcards.prompt: Are CCPA and consumer commissions the same institution?
flashcards.answer: No. The CCPA's statutory regulatory functions differ from the commissions' dispute-adjudication role.
flashcards.why: Match the function to the institution.

questions.stem: A question asks which provision is expressly framed for citizens rather than all persons. Which is the best answer?
options: Article 14
Article 19
Article 21
Article 300A
questions.explanation: Article 19 frames its listed freedoms for citizens; Articles 14 and 21 use person-based protection. Read the right-holder in the constitutional text.
questions.trap: Do not assume every constitutional protection has an identical holder.

questions.stem: Which statement about Article 32 is NOT correct?
options: It concerns the Supreme Court.
It concerns enforcement of Part III rights.
It is a general original remedy for every ordinary legal dispute.
Its constitutional text identifies writ remedies.
questions.explanation: Article 32 is tied to enforcement of Part III rights; its scope is not every ordinary dispute merely because a writ is requested.
questions.trap: The word NOT reverses the selection task.

questions.stem: An extract contrasts Supreme Court Part III enforcement with High Court writ jurisdiction for other legal purposes as well. Which pair best captures it?
options: Article 32 and Article 226
Article 14 and Article 15
Article 19 and Article 20
Article 37 and Article 51A
questions.explanation: The contrast is the subject scope of Articles 32 and 226. Territorial and jurisdictional requirements still apply to Article 226.
questions.trap: A familiar rights pair is not necessarily the jurisdiction pair.

questions.stem: A revision note describes Article 300A as a Part III fundamental right. What is the best correction?
options: It is not in the Constitution.
It only deals with personal liberty.
It is the same provision as Article 19(1)(a).
It is constitutional property protection outside Part III.
questions.explanation: Article 300A appears outside Part III. Being constitutional does not itself make a provision a Part III fundamental right.
questions.trap: Constitutional and fundamental are not interchangeable categories.

questions.stem: Both Houses of Parliament are in session. A draft is proposed under Article 123 solely to save legislative time. What is the clearest textual obstacle?
options: The sitting-condition restriction in Article 123.
Ordinances can never have legislative effect.
The President is not part of Parliament under Article 79.
All laws require a referendum.
questions.explanation: Article 123 excludes promulgation when both Houses are in session. Convenience does not remove this textual condition.
questions.trap: Check the condition before discussing duration or convenience.

questions.stem: Under Article 79, Parliament comprises which combination?
options: Only the Lok Sabha
The two Houses alone
The President and the two Houses
The Council of Ministers and State Governors
questions.explanation: Article 79 includes the President, the Council of States and the House of the People.
questions.trap: Constitutional composition differs from everyday shorthand.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Article 254(2) arrangement is NOT correct?
options: It concerns a specified inconsistency involving a State law.
Its presidential-assent arrangement permanently prevents later parliamentary law on that matter.
The provision includes a presidential-assent mechanism.
Its proviso preserves specified parliamentary lawmaking power.
questions.explanation: Article 254(2) does not permanently bar Parliament: its proviso preserves Parliament's power on the matter.
questions.trap: The distractor turns a qualified exception into absolute immunity.

questions.stem: A problem first asks whether a legislature has authority over the subject, then asks about inconsistency between laws. Which is the sound approach?
options: Treat both as identical questions about a minister's advice.
Apply Article 141 as if it were a distribution List.
Ignore the legislative field.
Separate competence under Article 246 from the specified inconsistency inquiry under Article 254.
questions.explanation: Legislative subject-matter competence and the operation of an inconsistency rule are distinct steps.
questions.trap: A correct conclusion on one step does not eliminate the other.

questions.stem: A proposal is defended by comparing benefits and harms to those affected. Which criterion most closely resembles Bentham's principle of utility?
options: The official's personal dislike
Its tendency to promote or diminish happiness
The age of the rule alone
The number of pages in the law
questions.explanation: Bentham evaluates the tendency of actions and governmental measures to affect happiness or welfare.
questions.trap: A decision-maker's preference is not the utility criterion.

questions.stem: In Bentham's calculus, extent directs attention to which matter?
options: How many persons are affected
Whether a command is printed
Whether the author is famous
Whether punishment is always imprisonment
questions.explanation: Extent brings the affected population into the assessment.
questions.trap: Do not confuse duration with the number of affected persons.

questions.stem: A passage distinguishes identifying existing law from assessing its moral merit. Which conclusion follows?
options: Every existing law is morally good.
Moral criticism of law is meaningless.
A rule can be identified as law and still morally criticised.
Every moral preference automatically becomes law.
questions.explanation: The distinction permits identification and criticism to be separate inquiries.
questions.trap: The wrong options replace a distinction with an absolute conclusion.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a sound way to answer an unfamiliar theory-passage inference question?
options: Identify the author's conclusion.
Check the supporting premises.
Look for limiting words.
Choose a familiar slogan even when the passage contradicts it.
questions.explanation: An inference must follow the actual passage rather than a memorised slogan. This is an original reading exercise, not an attributed legal doctrine.
questions.trap: Familiarity is not textual support.

questions.stem: A decision-maker hears both parties fully but has an alleged disqualifying personal interest in the result. Which separate concern remains?
options: Absence of any hearing
Impartiality of the decision-maker
Whether the statute was printed in blue
The number of pages filed
questions.explanation: The hearing requirement and impartiality are distinct. A full hearing does not by itself answer the separate interest/bias concern.
questions.trap: Do not let satisfaction of one requirement conceal another.

questions.stem: What is the best description of audi alteram partem?
options: A full jury trial is mandatory in every administrative matter.
Every adverse decision is unlawful.
A fair opportunity to answer the material case, in a context-appropriate form.
Only the decision-maker may see the case.
questions.explanation: The principle concerns an effective opportunity to be heard; the required procedure is contextual.
questions.trap: The principle is not a universal identical-trial requirement.

questions.stem: Which statement is NOT a reliable procedural-fairness inference?
options: An adverse outcome alone does not prove unfairness.
Impartiality and hearing are distinct.
The actual notice and adverse material matter.
A person who loses must necessarily have been denied a fair hearing.
questions.explanation: Losing and being denied a fair opportunity are separate propositions.
questions.trap: Do not infer a procedural defect from the outcome alone.

questions.stem: A licensing applicant is invited to respond, but the only decisive adverse report is concealed. What should an exam analysis examine first?
options: Whether there was a meaningful opportunity to address the material case.
Whether any letter called hearing was sent, which always ends the inquiry.
Whether the applicant likes the final result.
Whether every administrative hearing must have a jury.
questions.explanation: The content of the opportunity and the material case matter, not merely the hearing label. Context still controls the precise legal requirements.
questions.trap: A formal invitation need not resolve every fairness issue.

questions.stem: A card says: I sincerely believed my conduct was lawful, so BNS good faith is automatically established. What is the best response?
options: Correct, sincerity always suffices.
The question belongs only to contract law.
Section 2(11) also requires due care and attention; the relevant exception must be identified.
Every mistake of law is automatically excused.
questions.explanation: The BNS definition makes due care and attention relevant, and particular exceptions have particular conditions.
questions.trap: Honesty is not a substitute for the full statutory test.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly identifies the principal subject?
options: BNSS — criminal procedure
BSA — contract formation
BNS — consumer commissions
IPC — current electronic-record certification procedure under BSA
questions.explanation: BNSS concerns criminal procedure. BNS concerns substantive criminal law and BSA evidence.
questions.trap: Attach the enactment to the section number.

questions.stem: Which claim is NOT supported merely by the fact that a death has occurred?
options: A relevant offence inquiry may be needed.
Every ingredient of murder under BNS is established.
The applicable statutory conditions should be examined.
The facts and exceptions may affect classification.
questions.explanation: Death alone does not establish the full ingredients and absence of relevant exceptions required by the applicable offence.
questions.trap: An outcome cannot replace the legal test.

questions.stem: A student uses an official IPC-to-BNS table. What is its safest use?
options: It proves every mapped provision is word-for-word identical.
It abolishes every savings question.
It makes all older factual contexts irrelevant.
It helps locate provisions for comparison; wording and temporal application still need checking.
questions.explanation: A correspondence table is a navigation tool, not a substitute for the law's text, commencement or savings provisions.
questions.trap: A mapping is not a finding of complete legal equivalence.

questions.stem: A confession to a police officer is described as voluntary. Under the BSA, which is the best starting response?
options: Voluntariness automatically permits proof of every confession.
Section 23(1) supplies a separate restriction that must be considered.
No rule governs police confessions.
The answer depends only on whether it was handwritten.
questions.explanation: Section 23(1) is a separate rule; voluntariness does not by itself answer it.
questions.trap: Do not collapse all confession rules into one test.

questions.stem: Which part does the BSA discovery proviso allow to be proved in the specified circumstances?
options: Every statement made during the investigation.
Every confession by any person.
Only information distinctly related to the discovered fact.
Only the police officer's unrelated opinion.
questions.explanation: The proviso is limited; it does not automatically admit the whole accompanying narrative.
questions.trap: The exception must retain its boundaries.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a safe general proposition?
options: A logically relevant fact automatically makes every proposed method of proving it lawful.
Specific proof rules can matter.
Burden rules concern who must establish facts.
Savings can matter to pending older proceedings.
questions.explanation: Relevance and permissible proof must be considered separately.
questions.trap: Relevance is not a universal bypass of admissibility requirements.

questions.stem: Which question reflects the practical BSA section 105 burden test?
options: Which lawyer arrived first?
Which party produced the longest pleading?
Which party is most confident?
Who would fail if neither side gave evidence?
questions.explanation: Section 105 uses the no-evidence test to locate the burden.
questions.trap: Procedure order or confidence does not replace the statutory inquiry.

questions.stem: A named breach amount appears in a contract. What does Contract Act section 74 make the sound starting position?
options: The named amount must always be awarded automatically.
Only criminal punishment can follow.
Reasonable compensation is assessed within the statutory ceiling.
The existence of any named amount voids the agreement.
questions.explanation: Section 74 concerns reasonable compensation not exceeding the named amount or stipulated penalty.
questions.trap: A maximum is not an automatic award.

questions.stem: Under section 2(d), consideration at the promisor's desire may move from whom?
options: Only a court
Only the promisee, never anyone else
Only the government
The promisee or another person
questions.explanation: The Indian statutory definition expressly includes the promisee or another person.
questions.trap: Avoid importing a different legal system's formula.

questions.stem: Which statement is NOT correct?
options: Payment by itself cures any unlawful object under section 23.
A contract is an agreement enforceable by law.
Free consent and competence are separate conditions.
Section 25 includes specified exceptions.
questions.explanation: Lawfulness is a separate enforceability question; payment cannot by itself remove an unlawful object.
questions.trap: One satisfied element cannot replace all others.

questions.stem: A purported acceptance changes a material term in the offer. Which rule is most directly relevant?
options: Every proposal is automatically a completed contract.
Section 7's absolute-and-unqualified acceptance requirement.
Article 123 ordinance duration.
The definition of consumer commission.
questions.explanation: Section 7 makes the nature of acceptance a specific inquiry. Changing a material term is not simply unqualified assent to the offer.
questions.trap: Calling a reply acceptance does not determine its legal character.

questions.stem: A fictional negligence claim establishes a duty and a careless act, but no causally connected legally recognised damage. What is the best diagnosis?
options: All elements are automatically established.
The claimant's confidence supplies damage.
Consumer law necessarily replaces the inquiry.
The negligence chain still lacks a required element.
questions.explanation: The basic structure requires resulting damage causally connected with breach as well as duty and breach.
questions.trap: Do not stop after identifying carelessness.

questions.stem: Which pair best matches the Consumer Protection Act vocabulary?
options: Goods shortcoming — deficiency; service shortcoming — ordinance
Goods shortcoming — defect; service shortcoming — deficiency
Goods shortcoming — writ; service shortcoming — charge
Both always mean a criminal conviction
questions.explanation: The statutory definitions distinguish defect in goods and deficiency in services. The definitions still have to be applied to facts.
questions.trap: Similar complaint language can refer to different defined objects.

questions.stem: Which statement is NOT a sound use of the livelihood/self-employment explanation?
options: Its statutory limits matter.
The purpose and manner of use require examination.
It exempts every business purchase merely because a business earns income.
It concerns the specified use of goods for livelihood through self-employment.
questions.explanation: The explanation is limited; it is not a general exemption for all income-generating commercial transactions.
questions.trap: Do not generalise a bounded exception.

questions.stem: What is the best institutional distinction?
options: CCPA's statutory regulatory role differs from consumer commissions' adjudicatory role.
CCPA is simply another name for every District Commission.
Consumer commissions enact constitutional amendments.
CCPA and Parliament are identical.
questions.explanation: They have different functions under the consumer-protection framework.
questions.trap: Match functions rather than similar consumer-protection labels.

passages.title: The rights clinic’s jurisdiction mix-up
passages.passage: A fictional university legal clinic is sorting three requests. A visitor alleges that a public authority has violated a Part III right. Another visitor complains only about a statutory entitlement and supplies no allegation of a fundamental-right violation. A third asks the clinic to describe every constitutional provision as a fundamental right. The supervisor asks the students to keep classification separate from the desirability of a remedy. She explains that Article 32 concerns Supreme Court enforcement of Part III rights, while Article 226 gives High Courts a wider subject scope, including other legal purposes, subject to its own jurisdictional requirements. She also notes that Article 300A is constitutional property protection outside Part III. The class must not decide a real dispute from these short descriptions: the exact facts, territorial requirements and available legal procedures still matter. One student writes that adding the word writ to a complaint automatically establishes Article 32 jurisdiction. Another writes that the wider wording of Article 226 means no limits exist at all. The supervisor rejects both shortcuts. For each request she asks for three separate entries: the right claimed, the constitutional location of that right, and the jurisdictional route that the text could support.

questions.stem: Which clinic note most clearly misstates Article 32?
options: It concerns Part III enforcement.
Every statutory entitlement automatically falls within it once called a writ.
The right claimed should be identified.
Jurisdiction should be checked.
questions.explanation: Article 32 concerns enforcement of Part III rights; merely using the word writ does not turn an ordinary statutory dispute into a fundamental-right claim.
questions.trap: A remedy label cannot replace the jurisdictional condition.

questions.stem: What distinction does the supervisor draw about Article 300A?
options: It is a company-law provision.
It is a tax rate.
It protects property constitutionally outside Part III.
It abolishes every statutory property remedy.
questions.explanation: The passage identifies Article 300A as constitutional protection outside Part III, not as a Part III fundamental right.
questions.trap: Constitutional status and fundamental-right status are not identical.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is NOT supported by the passage?
options: The exact facts matter.
Article 226 has wider subject scope.
The right and remedy should be separated.
Article 226 has no jurisdictional limits.
questions.explanation: The passage expressly qualifies the wider Article 226 scope by its own jurisdictional requirements.
questions.trap: Do not remove the qualification while retaining the broad rule.

passages.title: An altered acceptance and a named sum
passages.passage: In this original classroom problem, Asha offers to supply a specified set of desks to Bina for an agreed price and delivery date. Bina replies that she accepts only if the price is reduced and a new service is included. The tutor asks students not to begin with damages. First they must decide whether the reply is an absolute and unqualified acceptance of the proposed terms. The exercise then supplies a separate assumption: suppose a valid contract is later made, a breach occurs, and the document names a sum payable on breach. The class must now consider the statutory compensation framework rather than assume the printed sum is automatically recovered in every case. Section 74 speaks to reasonable compensation within its statutory ceiling. The tutor also reminds students that the lawfulness of an agreement’s object is a separate question under section 23; payment alone cannot cure an unlawful object. None of the fictional parties is asking for advice about a real transaction. The purpose is to identify the stage of analysis. Formation, lawful object, breach and remedy are related, but answering one does not silently establish every other element. Students must state the relevant rule before testing each altered fact.

questions.stem: Which rule should first be considered for Bina’s changed terms?
options: Section 7 on absolute and unqualified acceptance
Only the amount of damages
Only the company’s incorporation
ICJ party standing
questions.explanation: The reply changes material terms. Section 7 supplies the acceptance inquiry before the later remedy assumption is reached.
questions.trap: Do not skip formation and begin with damages.

questions.stem: Under the separate valid-contract assumption, what is the section 74 starting point?
options: Automatic recovery of any named sum
Reasonable compensation within the statutory ceiling
No compensation can ever be considered
The printed sum cures an unlawful object
questions.explanation: Section 74 is not a direction to award every named sum automatically. Its reasonable-compensation framework and ceiling matter.
questions.trap: A ceiling and an automatic entitlement are different.

questions.stem: Which statement is NOT supported?
options: Legal stages should be separated.
The altered facts matter.
Payment alone cures every unlawful object.
A remedy question can follow an assumed valid contract.
questions.explanation: Section 23’s lawful-object inquiry is not cured merely by payment. The passage expressly separates the inquiries.
questions.trap: Do not treat performance or payment as a universal legality cure.

passages.title: The confession and the discovery note
passages.passage: A fictional evidence seminar compares two statements in a problem expressly governed by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam. The first is described as a voluntary confession to a police officer. A student assumes that the word voluntary ends the inquiry. The instructor asks the class to inspect section 23 separately rather than collapse every confession rule into the question of inducement. The second statement is information received from an accused person in police custody and is followed by a discovered fact. The instructor adds that the statutory discovery proviso is limited: it does not convert every part of a long narrative into admissible proof merely because something was eventually found. The class should identify the portion distinctly related to the discovered fact and check the prescribed circumstances. The seminar then distinguishes the relevance of a proposition from the legality of the method used to prove it. A relevant subject does not make every proposed statement or document automatically admissible. Finally, the class is told to preserve the governing legal version. An older examination question naming the Indian Evidence Act should be analysed as written, while a current-version comparison should be made openly, with its wording and savings checked separately.

questions.stem: Why does the label voluntary not end the first inquiry?
options: Every voluntary statement is irrelevant.
The BSA has no confession rules.
A police confession raises the separate section 23 restriction.
All old and new provisions have identical numbering.
questions.explanation: The section 23 restriction must be considered independently; voluntariness alone does not remove the police-officer issue.
questions.trap: Do not replace one statutory condition with another.

questions.stem: What is the limited discovery focus described in the passage?
options: The whole story in every case
Every allegation in a police file
Any sentence with a date
The information distinctly related to the discovered fact in the specified circumstances
questions.explanation: The discovery proviso is limited to the relevant portion and statutory circumstances, not the entire surrounding narrative.
questions.trap: A discovery does not validate every part of a statement.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a safe revision method?
options: Silently substituting every old section number with a guessed new one
Checking the statute named
Separating relevance and admissibility
Checking the actual discovery circumstances
questions.explanation: The passage requires legal-version care and a transparent comparison, not guessed substitutions.
questions.trap: Similarity of topic is not proof of identical wording or numbering.

passages.title: The licence decision and the unseen report
passages.passage: This original fictional scenario concerns an authority deciding whether a licence should continue. The affected person receives a short invitation to submit comments, but the authority relies decisively on an adverse report that it does not identify or disclose in the exercise. The classroom problem supplies no statutory emergency exception. One student says that sending any invitation necessarily establishes a fair hearing. A second says that losing the licence necessarily proves unfairness. The tutor asks both to focus on whether there was a meaningful opportunity to address the material case in the relevant context. She then changes one fact: the person receives the material and can respond, but the decision-maker has an alleged disqualifying personal interest in the result. This raises an impartiality question distinct from the opportunity to respond. The tutor does not promise that every fairness problem requires an identical oral procedure or an identical remedy. The governing law, the setting and any supported exception must be examined. The exercise’s purpose is to separate the existence of a genuine response opportunity, the independence of the decision-maker and the substantive correctness of the eventual decision. Each proposition needs its own reasoning rather than a slogan.

questions.stem: Which question best addresses the unseen decisive report?
options: Was any invitation sent, regardless of content?
Was there a meaningful opportunity to answer the material case?
Did the applicant necessarily have to win?
Was the authority’s name familiar?
questions.explanation: The focus is a meaningful opportunity to address the material relied on, within the relevant legal context. A formal invitation alone may not answer it.
questions.trap: Form and substance of an opportunity can differ.

questions.stem: What distinct concern arises from the changed personal-interest fact?
options: Patent duration
Share ownership
Impartiality of the decision-maker
The GST Council’s membership
questions.explanation: A disqualifying interest raises an impartiality issue even if a response opportunity has been provided.
questions.trap: Hearing and absence of bias are separate safeguards.

questions.stem: Which proposition does the passage reject?
options: Context matters.
The governing law should be checked.
Remedy and correctness are separate questions.
Every losing party necessarily received an unfair hearing.
questions.explanation: Losing does not itself prove procedural unfairness; the adequacy of the procedure requires its own examination.
questions.trap: Do not infer procedure solely from an unwelcome result.
